claims.text: Formation and retention of protective oxide layers in high-temperature HEAs is primarily controlled by preferential oxidation of selected constituent elements.
Atomic size and redox potential govern the initial oxidation stages of equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn.
Redox potential becomes the dominant influence on oxidation behavior over time in equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn.
Elements having lower redox potential and favorable atomic size oxidize preferentially.
Chromium is a key preferentially oxidized element in the proposed CoCrFeNiMn system.
Time-dependent oxidation causes composition inversion at the alloy surface.
Preferential oxidation produces a continuous oxide scale dominated by the oxide of the preferentially oxidized element.
The resulting oxide scale is adherent.
The resulting oxide scale is self-healing.
The oxide scale acts as a barrier that retards oxygen diffusion into the alloy bulk.
Restricting oxygen ingress slows subsequent oxidation and provides oxidation resistance.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn undergoes oxidation-induced surface compositional and structural changes in a controlled oxygen environment.
The standard CoCrFeNiMn alloy will develop a uniform protective oxide layer under the proposed high-temperature oxidation conditions.
Reducing or substituting the key reactive element will produce a thinner, more discontinuous, or less protective scale than the standard alloy.
Changing the key reactive-element concentration will measurably alter oxidation kinetics relative to the standard alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily above 800 degrees Celsius in oxygen-rich conditions.
The mechanism may not apply at lower temperatures or in substantially different atmospheres.
The standard alloy's balanced elemental composition promotes preferential formation of the protective oxide.
